title: Odile and the Uniform
premise: In 1913, Ivo Quintana drives for suffragist Odile Marchetti and secretly reads every letter she dictates, memorizing the names of women whose petitions vanish into official ledgers. When the army requisitions their town to build a munitions depot, a requisition ledger containing those very names falls into Ivo's hands, making him both courier and target. As soldiers occupy the workshop where Odile's movement prints its pamphlets, Ivo must copy and redistribute the names before the building—and the record of every woman who dared sign—is destroyed. The novel ends on New Year's Eve 1913 with the workshop burned but the names scattered across the country in a thousand envelopes, Ivo finally signing his own name beside them.
about_author: Lena Okafor is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing confiscated correspondence from early twentieth-century political movements. She writes historical fiction about the people history files under 'assistant.'

chapters.title: The Man Behind the Wheel
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Establishes his routine: driving Odile to meetings, sorting her mail, reading letters he shouldn't. He tells himself it's efficiency, not curiosity. Emotional beat: quiet loneliness disguised as professionalism; the first hint that the letters contain something worth protecting.

chapters.title: A Ledger of Names
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She dictates responses to petitioners while Ivo listens from the doorway. We learn the master ledger holds four hundred signatures of women demanding the vote—signatures that have already cost some of them their jobs. Emotional beat: Odile's fierce tenderness toward strangers; Ivo's growing sense of complicity.

chapters.title: Requisition Notice
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Soldiers post notices: the town's eastern quarter, including Marchetti's print workshop, is seized for a munitions depot. Evacuation in thirty days. Emotional beat: disbelief curdling into dread as Ivo realizes what stands inside that building besides presses.

chapters.title: What the Colonel Wants
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. A courteous colonel offers Odile safe passage if she surrenders 'party materials.' She smiles and agrees to nothing. That night she shows Ivo the ledger for the first time. Emotional beat: two conspirators recognizing each other at last.

chapters.title: Thirty Days
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. They plan: copy all four hundred names by hand, mail them to sympathetic contacts nationwide before the deadline. Ivo volunteers his route knowledge as a driver. Emotional beat: fear transformed into purpose; the found family of the workshop begins to cohere.

chapters.title: The Typesetter's Daughter
chapters.summary: Marta's POV (introduced). Sixteen, sharp-eyed, she catches Ivo copying pages and instead of betraying him, demands to help. Her father died in a press accident the army now calls 'an industrial matter.' Emotional beat: grief finding an outlet; the circle widens.

chapters.title: Checkpoints
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. First smuggling run: envelopes hidden in the spare tire and under Marta's coat. A young sergeant searches the car and finds nothing—but takes Ivo's papers for 'verification.' Emotional beat: the noose tightening; Ivo understands he can no longer be invisible.

chapters.title: Letters We Never Sent
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Flashback chapter: how Odile came to collect names, and the sister she lost to a factory fire no one was punished for. Justice outside the law is her creed. Emotional beat: the moral spine of the book revealed; Ivo listens and finally speaks his own history.

chapters.title: The Sergeant's Doubt
chapters.summary: Sergeant Brandt's POV (introduced). Ordered to surveil the workshop, he reads a confiscated pamphlet and recognizes his own mother's situation in it. He returns Ivo's papers without filing the incident report. Emotional beat: the enemy is not monolithic; mercy has a cost Brandt hasn't yet paid.

chapters.title: Two Hundred and Sixty-One
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. Copying marathon in the cellar; they're past halfway when a name stops Marta cold—a neighbor who denounced her father. Debate: include her or strike her? Odile rules: all names, or none. Emotional beat: the ethics of the archive; grace as discipline.

chapters.title: Intercepted
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. A mailbag is seized at the rail depot; eleven envelopes with workshop handwriting are burned publicly as a warning. The colonel announces inspections of all outgoing post. Emotional beat: humiliation and terror—but also proof someone upstairs is frightened of paper.

chapters.title: New Routes
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Improvisation: names sewn into garment hems, hidden in hymnals, carried by traveling saleswomen recruited through old suffragist networks. Marta volunteers for the most dangerous route. Emotional beat: ingenuity as resistance; the network becomes a living thing.

chapters.title: Brandt's Choice
chapters.summary: Sergeant Brandt's POV. His lieutenant orders a full search of the workshop within the week. Brandt must decide whether to warn them. He leaves an unsigned note under the workshop door. Emotional beat: conscience over career; the reader holds its breath.

chapters.title: The Last Three Hundred
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Race against the inspection: copying continues day and night while Marta trains three neighbors to carry. Ivo's hands cramp; Odile works beside him for the first time, copying her own detractors' wives. Emotional beat: exhaustion transfigured into solidarity.

chapters.title: Inspection Day
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The search comes. Presses dismantled, floorboards pried up—but the ledger sits in plain sight inside a broken piano the soldiers assume is furniture bound for scrap. Brandt watches, says nothing. Emotional beat: terror and absurd luck; the reader learns luck is often someone's silence.

chapters.title: What Brandt Paid
chapters.summary: Sergeant Brandt's POV. His warning note is traced; he's arrested for dereliction. From his cell window he sees the workshop lights burning late and understands they know. Emotional beat: sacrifice made visible; the cost of one decent man counted in days.

chapters.title: Evacuation Eve
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Final night. All but forty names are copied and dispatched. The army orders the workshop cleared by morning; demolition crews arrive at dawn. Odile refuses to leave until the last page is done. Emotional beat: defiance against arithmetic—the clock will not negotiate.

chapters.title: Fire
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. The army burns the building ahead of schedule, whether by accident or design never established. They watch from the hill road, the final forty names still uncopied, the ledger saved only because Ivo carried it out an hour before. Emotional beat: loss and fury; ashes as accusation.

chapters.title: Forty Names
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Hiding in a farmhouse, they finish the last copies by lamplight. Odile insists the final envelope go to Brandt's mother, so a soldier's family receives the truth too. Emotional beat: forgiveness extended beyond the obvious circle; the work completes itself morally.

chapters.title: New Year's Eve, 1913
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. In a borrowed hall, survivors of the network gather. Word arrives that a newspaper in a distant city has printed the full list of four hundred names. Cries, embraces, Marta laughing through tears. Emotional beat: vindication delayed but not denied; the century turns on their words.

chapters.title: The Signature
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Odile asks him to drive her north to restart the press somewhere new. Before leaving, Ivo does what he's never done: adds his own name to the ledger's margin—not as a petitioner, but as witness. Emotional beat: invisibility surrendered; belonging claimed.

chapters.title: Every Letter After
chapters.summary: Epilogue, mixed POV. Years later, Marta runs a print shop; Brandt, released, delivers her mail. Ivo still reads every letter first—now openly, as editor of the movement's correspondence. Emotional beat: the found family endures; justice, once begun outside the law, becomes ordinary daily work.
